name: sqlancer
why: Automatically finds logic bugs in database engines via generated queries, a fascinating look at how DBMS correctness is tested.

brief.what_it_is: SQLancer is a command-line Java tool that automatically tests database management systems for logic bugs, meaning cases where the DBMS returns an incorrect result set, such as silently omitting a record. It generates schemas, data, indexes, views, and queries in several phases, then checks the results with test oracles such as TLP, NoREC, PQS, DQP, and CODDTest. The input is a target DBMS, and the output is bug reports with log files containing the statements needed to reproduce each bug. It also covers performance issues via CERT and crash bugs. It supports many DBMSs, including SQLite3, DuckDB, H2, MySQL, PostgreSQL, and TiDB.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says SQLancer finds bugs in the DBMS implementation itself, not in user-written queries, and it presents logic bugs as its main focus. It states that it has found hundreds of bugs in mature, widely known DBMSs.
brief.how_it_works: SQLancer uses hand-written generators that work in phases: create a schema, insert data, add other database state, then generate queries. Each query is validated by a test oracle that compares results, for example by checking that a TLP partition or a NoREC rewrite matches the original query's result set. An optional feedback-guided mode (--qpg-enable, from QPG) mutates database state when no new query plans appear, to exercise more distinct plans. An experimental reducer (--use-reducer) applies delta debugging to shrink bug-inducing inputs.

brief.install_notes: Requires Java 11 or above and Maven. The README's main route is to clone the repo and run mvn package -DskipTests, then run the JAR from the target directory. Embedded DBMSs (DuckDB, H2, SQLite) need no separate install because their binaries come in as JAR dependencies. Other DBMSs need a running server. For those, SQLancer may expect a database named test to exist. Released JARs are on GitHub Releases, Maven Central, and DockerHub, but the README recommends the latest source version and says official releases are infrequent and irregular. Logs go to target/logs.
brief.standout: Rather than checking for crashes or hand-written expected results, it uses metamorphic and differential oracles, such as partitioning a query into three pieces or comparing a query with a rewrite that avoids optimizations. Its tests run in an infinite loop until a bug is found or a timeout is hit. Its lineage is academic, with a published paper behind almost every oracle, and the README links papers and talks.
brief.status: unknown. The README mentions 'As of January 2025' for the supported-DBMS list and lists a SIGMOD 2025 technique (CODDTest), which suggests recent activity. It also says the PQS approach is currently unmaintained, and the Twitter account is no longer maintained. The fetched README contains no release date or last-commit date, and I did not check the GitHub API or the releases page.
brief.caveats: Support depends on the DBMS version: the README says SQLancer targets a specific previous release, so newer versions can produce many AssertionErrors and false alarms. Some DBMSs are better supported than others. Non-English error locales can cause many failures. Crashes in embedded engines (DuckDB, H2, SQLite) will also crash the JVM. Without a bug, it runs forever unless you set --num-tries or --timeout-seconds. The reducer is experimental. The README says CERT findings are performance issues rather than clear-cut bugs. The license was not visible in the README, so I did not check it.

entry.title: SQLancer
entry.tldr: Fuzzes database engines like SQLite, DuckDB and PostgreSQL with generated queries, and uses clever oracles to catch cases where the database silently returns the wrong rows.
entry.deeper_look:
SQLancer is a Java command-line tool that tests database management systems for logic bugs: cases where the engine returns an incorrect result set, such as quietly dropping a row. It does not look at your queries. It looks for bugs in the DBMS implementation itself. The README says it has found hundreds of bugs in mature, widely used systems.

It works in phases. Hand-written generators create a schema, insert data, add indexes and views, then produce queries. Each query is checked by a test oracle. With TLP, a query is split into three partitions whose combined results must match the original. With NoREC, the query is compared against a rewrite that avoids the optimizer. Other oracles include PQS, DQP and CODDTest. There are also modes for performance issues (CERT) and crashes.

The idea underneath is metamorphic testing. You rarely know the correct answer to a random query, but you can know that two different formulations of it must agree. If they do not, one is wrong, and the log files contain the statements needed to reproduce it. Almost every oracle has a published paper behind it, and the README links to them, so the tool doubles as a reading list on how database correctness gets tested.

Optional extras include a feedback-guided mode (`--qpg-enable`) that mutates database state to reach new query plans, and an experimental reducer (`--use-reducer`) that shrinks bug-inducing inputs with delta debugging.
entry.install:
brew install sqlancer
# Needs Java (brew pulls in openjdk). The README's main route is instead: git clone the repo, then build with Maven (Java 11+ and Maven required).
# Embedded DBMSs (SQLite, DuckDB, H2) need nothing else. Others need a running server, and some expect a database named test.

entry.whats_unique: Instead of looking for crashes or comparing against hand-written expected results, it uses metamorphic and differential oracles, so it can detect wrong answers with no known right answer. Nearly every oracle comes with an academic paper.
entry.caveats: It targets specific DBMS versions, so newer releases can produce false alarms, and without a bug it runs forever unless you set --num-tries or --timeout-seconds.
